newsitem.title: GUAM: S. Korean jet crashes in Guam, about 200 dead.
newsitem.headline: S. Korean jet crashes in Guam, about 200 dead.

text.p: About 200 people died when a South Korean jumbo jet crashed and burst into flames on this U.S. Pacific island early on Wednesday, but several people survived, including a woman who walked away unscathed.

The Korean Air Lines Boeing 747 flying mostly South Korean tourists and honeymooners from Seoul crashed in a rugged jungle area and ruptured an oil pipeline just miles (km) from the airport and not far from the island's most heavily populated area.
The plane tried to land in a torrential downpour.

Guam Gov. Carl Gutierrez said 35 people had been pulled alive from the wreckage but three had subsequently died. But Korean Air Lines officials said 55 people had been saved and 27 had been admitted to hospital.
There was no immediate confirmation on Guam of the figures given by the airline in Seoul.

Giving the first official death toll, Gutierrez said about 200 people had lost their lives. "It's a tragedy," he said, describing how he had personally helped to save five people from the burning plane.
He said the crash scene was pitch black and rescuers had to follow the screams of survivors.

"The fire (from the plane) was not so big, so we had to follow the sounds. It was eerie and as we got closer I heard all the screams coming from the dark spots ... We had to follow the sounds," he said in a conference call with reporters.
Gutierrez said the plane burst into flames after hitting an oil pipeline that runs through the rugged jungle area islanders call the "boondocks" just outside of the capital.

Airline officials said Korean Air Lines Flight 801 was carrying 231 passengers and 23 crewmembers, including dozens of vacationers, several South Korean politicians, three infants and at least 13 Americans.

Gutierrez said one woman walked away unscathed from the crash save for a few scratches. Guam Memorial Hospital doctor Edwardo Cruz said the woman was a stewardess who said the plane started to shake just before the crash. The shaking was followed by a big bang, he quoted her as saying.
Gutierrez, one of the first people to reach the crash scene, said he saved five people, including a Korean mother and daughter who "wouldn't let go of each other."
He added, "They were embedded into the steel and the cushions." Eventually, a doctor "yanked" the girl out and the mother followed her, he said.
Gutierrez also pulled out an 11-year-old Japanese girl but flames stopped him from going back into the wreckage to save her mother. "The mother was dead in the flames," Gutierrez said.
Guam and other Pacific islands are popular destinations for South Korean honeymooners.
Airline officials said Shin Ki-ha, a former South Korean parliamentary leader of the opposition National Congress for New Politics, his wife and 20 party members were on the plane.
The aircraft broke into several pieces with people in the middle section dying almost instantly in the flames.
The plane's black box flight recorder was recovered and was being flown to Hawaii for analysis, the governor said.
The National Transportation Safety Board has started a probe into the cause of the crash, chairman Jim Hall said.
He told a Seattle news conference that investigators would be looking into why a vital piece of airport safety equipment was not in service for the landing.
Hall said officials on Guam had confirmed that the airport's glide slope, a device used for instrument landing during poor visibility, had been out of service for some time.
But he added that instrument landings could be made without the glide slope.
Air safety sources said visibility at the time was limited to about one mile (1.6 km) due to the heavy rain.
Dr. Cruz said staff at Guam Memorial Hospital watched the flaming wreckage from the hospital.
"We didn't hear anything, but we walked out and looked up and there was a big fireball on the mountain," Cruz said.
Ginger Cruz, spokeswoman for Gutierrez, said some survivors had broken limbs and the most serious ones were immediately taken to hospitals by helicopter.
A massive rescue effort was launched by the U.S. Navy and local civil defence and emergency services using U.S. Sea Knight helicopters and bulldozers to cut through the jungle.
An FAA spokeswoman said the plane had just been cleared for landing at 2:35 a.m. local time on Wednesday (12:35 p.m. EDT on Tuesday) (1635 GMT on Tuesday) when radar contact was lost.
An emergency field hospital was set up by U.S. Navy personnel as close to the wreckage as possible.
Gutierrez said conditions for rescue workers were very difficult and muddy. He said the area was very slippery and grass grew to shoulder height.
Bulldozers carved out a road for emergency vehicles.

Guam, largest of the Mariana Islands in the Western Pacific, is an unincorporated territory of the United States with a population of about 144,000. A U.S. military base covers about one-third of the island, the westernmost U.S. territory, which is located 4,000 miles (6,437 km) west of Hawaii and 2,200 miles (3,540 km) south east of Seoul.
